newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela pledges privatisation, ending fx controls.
newsitem.headline: Mandela pledges privatisation, ending fx controls.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela on Friday pledged his government's commitment to the privatisation of key state assets and reaffirmed its commitment to the phased removal of foreign exchange controls.
However, he gave no details on how and when restrictions on taking currency out of the country would be lifted.

Addressing the opening of the 1997 session of parliament, Mandela said the government was accelerating implementation of its macro-economic plan, adding he believed the country had turned the corner towards consistent economic expansion.
Commenting on plans for ending foreign exchange controls on residents -- which have been the subject of intense speculation in the run-up to Friday's speech -- Mandela said:
"I would...like to reaffirm our commitment to the phased removal of remaining exchange controls."
Mandela said the restructuring and privatisation of state assets was a critical part of the government's Growth, Employment and Redistribution (GEAR) programme, unveiled last June.
"In a matter of months...Telkom will acquire a strategic equity partner and Sunair and (resorts group) Aventura will be wholly privatised," he said.
"The Airports Company and (forestry group) Safcol should complete thier bidding processes this year. Alexcor (a diamond mining company) is also being attended to."

Restructuring state-owned companies inherited from the apartheid era was a pivotal part of the government's plan to attract investment and technology, ensure efficiency and guarantee affordable prices, he said.
"In the overall we are confident that we have moved into high gear in the implementation of the macro-economic strategy," he said.
Mandela painted an upbeat picture of the South African economy, although he acknowledged growth was insufficient to absorb the number of jobseekers entering the market each year.
"With the estimated three percent growth during the course of last year, the South African economy has turned the cornrer towards consistent expansion," he said.
"Beneath this figure, which is of course less than what all of us would prefer, are strong signals of a robust industrial revolution in the marking."

South Africa was seeing many investment projects of over 500 million rand each, together with phenomenal growth in fixed investments, improved capacity utilisation and physical volume of production and a steep rise in manufactured exports.
Mandela added he was confident that new labour relations legislation should temper conflicts in the workplace.

"Although no one piece of legislation can be a panacea to our deep social prblems, this new regime should temper conflicts at the workplace and help strengthen the partnership between business and labour in national development," he said.
The country's fiscal and monetary authorities had performed well to ensure the country met its targeted budget figures, despite exchange rate pressures, he said.
During 1997 the government would complete plans towards medium term budgeting in order to bring budget allocations closer to strategic objectives and speed up reprioritisation within departments.
"We will also intensify efforts to improve the government's management of cash flows and eliminate unnecessary burdens on the fiscus," he said.

"I also wish to emphasis that in our efforts as government to ensure that the nation lives within its means we will take into account our mandate to the electorate, particularly the social requirements of the present and the future and the benefits that will accrue from bold decisions."
Commenting on South Africa's alarming crime rate, Mandela said progress was being made via the National Crime Prevention Strategy.

"Despite the difficulties, despite the fact that such achievements mean little to those who still experience crime, the fact of the matter is that the offensive is on, particularly with regard to most priority crimes. Government is confident of making further progress in the fight for safety, security and stability."
